problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

a. Verdict: I have successfully solved the problem. The final answer is 4048.

b. Method Sketch:
1. Show that the uncovered squares must form a permutation matrix; by permuting rows and columns we may assume they lie on the main diagonal.
2. Prove that any axis-aligned rectangle that avoids the diagonal must lie entirely either above or below it, so the upper and lower triangular regions can be tiled independently.
3. Construct a tiling with exactly 2n-2 rectangles: for each row i (1 <= i <= n-1) place a horizontal 1 by (n-i) rectangle covering cells (i, i+1) through (i, n); for each column j (1 <= j <= n-1) place a vertical (n-j) by 1 rectangle covering cells (j+1, j) through (n, j). Verify that these rectangles are disjoint and cover all non-diagonal cells.
4. Prove a lower bound of 2n-2 rectangles. For each inner diagonal point (k,k) with 1 <= k <= n-1, the cell to its right (k,k+1) must be covered by a rectangle whose lower-left corner is the grid point (k+1,k+1); similarly the cell below (k+1,k) forces a rectangle with upper-right corner at (k,k). Thus each inner diagonal point is a corner of a rectangle, and a rectangle can contain at most one such inner corner. Hence at least n-1 rectangles are needed above the diagonal and at least n-1 below, giving a total of at least 2n-2.
5. Since the construction meets the lower bound, the minimum number of tiles is 2n-2. For n = 2025 this equals 4048.

### Detailed Solution ###
1. Uncovered squares form a permutation matrix.
Number the rows 1,2,...,n and the columns 1,2,...,n with n = 2025. The condition that each row contains exactly one uncovered unit square and each column also contains exactly one uncovered square implies that the set U of uncovered squares consists of n squares, no two sharing a row or a column. Therefore there exists a permutation sigma of {1,2,...,n} such that
U = { (i, sigma(i)) | i = 1,2,...,n }.
Here (i,j) denotes the unit square in row i and column j.

2. Reduction to the diagonal case.
If we permute the rows according to any permutation tau and the columns according to any permutation pi, the problem does not change: rectangles remain rectangles aligned with the grid, and the condition "exactly one uncovered square in each row and column" is preserved. By applying the column permutation pi(j) = sigma^{-1}(j) (leaving rows unchanged) we map the set U to the main diagonal
D = { (i,i) | 1 <= i <= n }.
Thus it suffices to solve the problem for the diagonal configuration; the minimal number of tiles for the original configuration is the same as for the diagonal case.

3. Geometry of the remaining cells.
After removing the diagonal squares, the board consists of two disjoint regions:
Upper region U_T = { (i,j) | 1 <= i < j <= n } (strictly above the diagonal),
Lower region L_T = { (i,j) | 1 <= j < i <= n } (strictly below the diagonal).
Consider any axis-aligned rectangle R whose sides lie on grid lines and which is required to avoid the diagonal squares. Let the rows of R be the interval [r1, r2] and the columns the interval [c1, c2] (both inclusive). If R contained a cell both above and below the diagonal, then the intervals [r1, r2] and [c1, c2] would intersect, and the cell (k,k) with k in the intersection would belong to R, contradicting the avoidance of the diagonal. Hence either r2 < c1 (the rectangle lies entirely above the diagonal) or c2 < r1 (the rectangle lies entirely below the diagonal). Consequently the upper and lower regions can be tiled independently.

4. A tiling with 2n-2 tiles.
We now exhibit a tiling of the two regions using exactly 2n-2 rectangles.

Upper region.
For each i in {1,2,...,n-1} define the horizontal tile
H_i = { (i,j) | j = i+1, i+2, ..., n }.
H_i is a 1 by (n-i) rectangle; it lies entirely above the diagonal because its only row is i and its leftmost column is i+1 > i.

Lower region.
For each j in {1,2,...,n-1} define the vertical tile
V_j = { (i,j) | i = j+1, j+2, ..., n }.
V_j is a (n-j) by 1 rectangle; it lies entirely below the diagonal because its only column is j and its topmost row is j+1 > j.

Verification of coverage.
Take any cell (r,c) with r < c (a cell of the upper region). Since c >= r+1, the cell belongs to H_r, because H_r contains exactly the cells (r,j) with j >= r+1. Thus every cell of the upper region is covered by exactly one horizontal tile.
Take any cell (r,c) with r > c (a cell of the lower region). Since r >= c+1, the cell belongs to V_c, because V_c contains exactly the cells (i,c) with i >= c+1. Thus every cell of the lower region is covered by exactly one vertical tile.

Verification of disjointness.
The horizontal tiles H_i are pairwise disjoint because they occupy distinct rows. The vertical tiles V_j are pairwise disjoint because they occupy distinct columns. Suppose a cell (i,j) belonged to both some H_i and some V_j. Then j > i (since H_i uses columns i+1 ... n) and simultaneously i > j (since V_j uses rows j+1 ... n), a contradiction. Hence no cell is covered by both a horizontal and a vertical tile. Consequently the 2n-2 tiles are disjoint and together cover all n^2 - n non-diagonal cells.

Thus a tiling with 2n-2 tiles exists.

5. A lower bound of 2n-2 tiles.
We now prove that no tiling can use fewer tiles.

Inner corners.
For each k in {1,2,...,n-1} consider the grid point (k,k). This point lies on the diagonal and is adjacent to the cell (k,k+1) to its right (in the upper region) and the cell (k+1,k) below it (in the lower region). In any tiling, the cell (k,k+1) must be covered by some rectangle R that lies entirely above the diagonal. Let R have row interval [r1, r2] and column interval [c1, c2]. Because R contains (k,k+1) we have r1 <= k <= r2 and c1 <= k+1 <= c2. Since R is above the diagonal we have r2 < c1. From k <= r2 < c1 <= k+1 we deduce r2 = k and c1 = k+1. Hence the lower-left corner of R is the grid point (k+1, k+1). An analogous argument shows that the rectangle covering the cell (k+1,k) (which lies in the lower region) has its upper-right corner at the grid point (k,k). Therefore each inner diagonal point (k,k) for 1 <= k <= n-1 is a corner of some rectangle.

At most one inner corner per rectangle.
Let R be a rectangle lying entirely above the diagonal. Its row interval is [r1, r2] and column interval [c1, c2] with r2 < c1. The four corners of R are (r1,c1), (r1,c2+1), (r2+1,c1), (r2+1,c2+1). Among these, the only one that can have equal coordinates is (r2+1, c1), because r2+1 <= c1 and equality holds exactly when c1 = r2+1. Thus a rectangle above the diagonal can contain at most one inner diagonal point, namely its lower-left corner. A rectangle below the diagonal is symmetric: its only possible inner diagonal point is its upper-right corner. Hence any rectangle can be responsible for at most one inner corner.

Counting inner corners.
There are n-1 inner diagonal points (k,k) with 1 <= k <= n-1. As shown above, each of them must be a corner of a rectangle, and each rectangle can serve at most one such point. Consequently at least n-1 rectangles are required to cover the upper region, and at least n-1 rectangles are required to cover the lower region. Therefore any tiling of the whole board needs at least (n-1)+(n-1) = 2n-2 rectangles.

6. Minimality and the answer for n = 2025.
The construction of Section 4 uses exactly 2n-2 rectangles, and the lower-bound argument of Section 5 shows that no tiling can use fewer. Hence the minimum possible number of tiles is 2n-2.
For n = 2025 we obtain
2*2025 - 2 = 4050 - 2 = 4048.
Thus the required minimum number of tiles is 4048.
